walkthroughs.body_html:
Formulae, Equations & Amounts — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Formulae, Equations & Amounts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Formulae, Equations & Amounts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A compound is 75% carbon and 25% hydrogen by mass. Its empirical formula is:
options: CH₄
CH₃
C₂H₆
CH₂

mcqs.q: How many moles of NaOH are in 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution?
options: 2.50 mol

mcqs.q: The empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is:
options: CH₂O
C₆H₁₂O₆
C₂H₄O₂
C₃H₆O₃

mcqs.q: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many moles of water form from 3 mol of H₂ with excess oxygen?
options: 3 mol
1.5 mol
6 mol
2 mol

mcqs.q: Does balancing an equation make the number of molecules equal on both sides?
options: No — it makes the number of atoms of each element equal on both sides; the molecule counts can differ.
Balancing means changing the formulae of compounds until they match.
A balanced equation must have the same number of molecules on each side.
Yields over 100% occur whenever a catalyst is used.

mcqs.q: If you double the volume of a solution at the same concentration, what happens to the moles of solute?
options: The moles halve because the solute is more spread out.
They double — n = c × V, so at fixed concentration the amount scales with volume.
The moles stay the same because the concentration has not changed.
Balancing means changing the formulae of compounds until they match.

mcqs.q: Can a percentage yield be greater than 100%?
options: A yield over 100% means the reaction worked better than expected.
No — an apparent yield over 100% signals an error, such as the product being wet or impure.
Balancing means changing the formulae of compounds until they match.
Yields over 100% occur whenever a catalyst is used.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Molecular formula”?
options: The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule; always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
The amount of solute in moles per cubic decimetre of solution; moles = concentration × volume in dm³.
The molar mass of the desired product divided by the total molar mass of all products, expressed as a percentage.
The actual amount of product obtained divided by the theoretical maximum, multiplied by one hundred.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Concentration”?
options: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound, found from masses or percentage composition.
One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles; the number of moles equals the mass divided by the molar mass.
The actual amount of product obtained divided by the theoretical maximum, multiplied by one hundred.
The amount of solute in moles per cubic decimetre of solution; moles = concentration × volume in dm³.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Empirical formula”?
options: The actual amount of product obtained divided by the theoretical maximum, multiplied by one hundred.
One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles; the number of moles equals the mass divided by the molar mass.
The amount of solute in moles per cubic decimetre of solution; moles = concentration × volume in dm³.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound, found from masses or percentage composition.

options: The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule; always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
The amount of solute in moles per cubic decimetre of solution; moles = concentration × volume in dm³.
One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles; the number of moles equals the mass divided by the molar mass.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound, found from masses or percentage composition.

options: The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule; always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.
One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles; the number of moles equals the mass divided by the molar mass.
The actual amount of product obtained divided by the theoretical maximum, multiplied by one hundred.
The molar mass of the desired product divided by the total molar mass of all products, expressed as a percentage.
